title: Ralph Emerson Brown and Jasper Taylor Interview, 1961-05-23
interviewee: Ralph Emerson Brown and Jasper Taylor

blocks.x: She was young I believe for the...
Somewhere I'd seen her besides the beautiful one. I don't remember where...
I mean her... She was a big old young girl, she was a big girl but she was young.
I don't believe she did.
She was good parents, she worked for most of the youngsters at that.
Do you remember that Jimmy Newman was at Rumbogie or was that while you were gone?
I think I was gone.
He broadcast from out there I think, but he had a fairly big band. You had five pieces.
I was in New York. I was in New York. When Rumbogie was open I was in New York. I lived here in 28.
Oh yeah, come to think but it was in the late 30s. Yeah, yeah.

I used to hear about Jimmy and his big band. He brought a nice size band to New York. They played for a while. But I'll tell you about their job at New York. A lot of people don't understand. See those folks at New York, you'd bring a small band in to some other place, they'd want to implement your band themselves. And they'd put fellows of their own liking with you.
That isn't a union requirement, they just like to build it.

They would do it, no, that wasn't a union requirement. I mean a union requirement if you play a theater, you have so many New York bands, outside bands, that's what that is. But those people in Sephora, they would mess around with your band, and they put a few fellows with Jimmy and his band, and it didn't do the band any good. I know that, see. One fellow named Big Green, Big Green's dead now, Big Trummel, there was a hard guy to get along with Snowy. He used to work for Fletcher Henderson, a hard guy, he liked to do just what he wanted to do. He could play like the devil when he wanted to. If he didn't play, he wouldn't play. And that hurt Jimmy, that hurt Jimmy a whole lot. A lot of people don't know, but that hurt Jimmy when they put different fellows in his band from New York. He had a small band, they heard his band, and they knew it was a small band, but after Savoy they decided his band should be bigger. Of course he did have to play against a big band, some fellow guy from Boston, and he was in a quite a sizable band. And of course Jimmy's small band didn't side with too good with it, let's say. But it didn't do the band any good for them to put two, three or four New York boys in there, because those New York guys are hard to have, I know them, see. And so Jimmy didn't stay Savoy too long, and it wasn't as small as he was.
That was before you left New York.

Yeah, yeah, yeah. I was in Savoy, I saw him in Savoy this morning. He's dropping out every night. I mean I had to drop in there just one night, and I think one of the boys told me, he said, he's about Mr. Jimmy's band putting these guys in there in his band. And I didn't do Jimmy's band any good, see Jimmy had his own style. And Jimmy is more of a small band man, you see, because he's playing soft, you know, that nice client, and a great big band doesn't do his style too good in the old way, see. He knows he's playing soft, you know, all guys can play suit themselves. You can't have those guys, see. So he didn't do his band any good.
Jimmy would work nicely with a big band around here because he'd use a microphone. Yeah. Oh yes. And when he was broadcasting, it sounds great.
Yeah, well see, these boys.
His own contribution was a little hard to find sometimes.

Oh yeah, well see, he could have these boys, you know, they'd play right soft on them, see. But those New York boys, they had those guys. Well there's some nice boys in New York, but there's some of them that you just can't do anything with.
Do you remember anybody besides Big Green who was with Jimmy?
Well I can't remember just now.
You don't know who was from Chicago. You don't remember Wally Bishop was with him? He played with him for a while. No, I can't say just who was with Jimmy.

I was in one night because I think I knew all this fellas. I think he took his regular six pieces I think he took to New York. He was six or maybe seven. I knew those fellas but right now I can't just call their names off. And he always had a nice band, six or seven pieces. I never heard this big band except I heard this guy here in New York, which wasn't his band, but the guys that they put in there.
Well Savoy had a lot of old favorites.
They had played with them for years. They knew certain musicians, they had certain favorites you know. Pick them in there. You've got to suit themselves most of the time.
Well Jimmy made out pretty well when he took a trio then and went to the West Post.
He did for all of them, yeah. As I say, he, a smaller band was more to his liking, I mean it's better, I think a small band, six or seven.
When he came from New Orleans did he make an impression right away? Was he able to play well enough that he decided he was a pretty good band?

Oh, Jimmy, Jimmy, Jimmy, as far as I know, Jimmy came out here, he was known as one of the best low-known men anywhere. He stayed at the low register and he was hit, as far as I know, he was hit. A lot of guys wanted him but he picked, he'd take some other band but he didn't like him, he didn't like the style of play, he wouldn't live. I heard him say many days, I didn't take those guys. He wasn't the kind of band he liked to play. A band that wasn't too noisy but he was at low register. I mean that's what made it. And of course he played well in the middle register. He never was a high register man, he could play but I mean he made his own low register. He had such technique and such a nice style.
Who were the other clarinets that impressed you around Chicago when you were here?
Oh, well Simeon, because Simeon died last year. Simeon was a great fellow, Donnell.
Simeon was pretty well developed when he came?

Oh yes, Simeon. Simeon played somewhat on Jimmy Noon's style. But they both, I guess they played together in the old ways. And of course now this fellow, Nichols, we used to play with Joe, Nichols and Bonnie, you know, because they were a great team.
An awful lot of clarinets came out of New Orleans.

Oh yes. Johnny Dodd. Johnny Dodd was a great soloist by himself, a high enough man. Now Bonnie and Bonnie, and Nichols, they were a great team because they played together. And I didn't know that they told me that Bonnie was a fellow that really knew the music. Nichols, they say he wasn't a great reader but I mean he was a great technique. But he and Bonnie played together. He was about the first of the real good clarinets teams. And they played saxophone too. That saxophone was mostly the instrument with Joe Alfa, they played clarinets too. But saxophone, they played the saxophone mostly. Bonnie was the first, the first tenor man I've heard. But most of the tenor man back in the early days, they played those cellopods, very meek, those cellopods you know. But Bonnie came in there playing at the Fayette saxophone. I don't know, I guess he and Stump came along about the same time I guess. He might have come in a little bit earlier than Stump. But I guess Stump would set a new style for bass and things.
Where has Hawkins been in? He was around Chicago for about a while.

Well he just came here with Fletcher's band. Well I think he was here even earlier maybe with Mamey Smith. Yes he did, he used to be a violin player. Years ago he started on violin, that's why he got to be a saxophone player. He came here with Mamey Smith and played in the grand theater.
Did he play violin with Mamey Smith? I don't think he did. I had an idea. Yeah, yeah.

Well Hawkins, like Duke, like Louis, a creator. And I always say that the imitators never, never greatest creators. To me Hawkins would always be the number one man. To me. A lot of those would come over and play a lot. A lot of those might blow Louis up. I mean Louis is still the king of that style. He's the creator. Hawkins was the creator of that fine saxophone player. A lot of them got a lot of good ones. But to me Hawkins has always number one. Always will be with Mamey.

In a sense I think that those clarinet players, Barney and Noon especially, were part of a family. In other words they were not especially creators even though they had great originality and you identify them immediately. They're of a family, maybe comes back from Teal. Teal and Bache.

Teal was probably the greatest of the Teal. He laid out in the style. Then Bache came along before he took up that old soprano sax. I never could see why Bache took that dog on soprano sax. Yet he made a whole lot of money with it. Well see people don't, they're lame like that's paying the bills, they don't know anything about what's going on.

Well actually it may have been the same sense of novelty that you noticed when you started off with an alto. It was a novel thing. Well it caught on to where it became a conventional instrument. Maybe the soprano could have become a conventional instrument instead of a bastard instrument but it has remained.

It was said, yeah but he played, people went for it. He said, see people like, people let's go for something that's offside. Yeah. But Bache, Clarnett, well that guy was a wonderful, wonderful, wonderful. Now he went overseas with a fellow named Will Mann Cook and Bache, never was a good reader. But Will Mann Cook was one of those particular guys.
He was on soprano by the time he went with Cook wasn't he? I think probably he was.

I thought he went with a listener on his clarinet but I thought, I'm not sure. But he set a good style for clarinet oh years ago. A good style for clarinet. And I don't know, maybe he saw so many clarinet players come along and he said, I'll take this soprano. And he took it and made God rich of it. But I had a lot of soprano saxophone. I just don't like to tell them what they had. Well of course I'm me about what does me, what I like or dislike. But Bache did some with it all right. But Charlotte Bonnet and a few others played in tune. Charlotte Bonnet and a few others played. Boyan Fields used to play with the . Those two folks played in tune.
You've heard Johnny Hodges play soprano.
Oh yes, Johnny does. He's old, he's fast, he's green light on soprano. Those three to me played in tune. But to me, Bache did ever play in tune. Maybe that's what took the people. You see them?
Oh yes, yes.

There's a lot of people, there's a lot of people who go for something that's just a little bit under what it should be. And a lot of these guys, some of these guys, we play in chord tones in certain things. But it seems like it's something that hits people. Something that's just a little bit offside.
Maybe get more emotional impact. I guess so, I guess so. Do you think Bache was mainly flat?

Well, it just seemed like it never seemed to be in tune to me. To me, he just never, he played with us out on Long Island, come out a couple of times, and played with us, just for fun of it. Of course, one time, I was playing in Long Island, Jeff Bache was, wasn't doing so good, he'd open up a place, a gambling place, and he'd lost all his money. He'd had money once, but he was broke at that time. And I don't know, I'd heard the guy play clarinet before, and just to me, maybe I was prejudiced. I'd heard him play this fine clarinet, and that old, that old, uh.
Well, he didn't play the clarinet out of tune as he did the soprano. Or you didn't notice it? No. I didn't know it. To me, he's just a natural kind of player. Just natural.

But the old soprano, I just never did it. Maybe it wasn't out of tune, but I just didn't like the old tone of it. To me, it wasn't a good tone. But what I call good tone, lots of other people, they like something that's a little, they call it a little weird or something. Just a little kind of off color. I guess there's something to it, because now, you take Glenn Miller and his fine arrangements, he used to carry a dissonant interval sometimes. It's all fine. But of course, those guys are all in tune. They had to be in tune to play that and sell those records. But he used to really carry, purposefully carry a dissonant interval in quite a bit of his arrangements. But he'd have these other ones down so low, and the other ones on top, but you could tell there's something odd about it. And people, it was still people's ease. I guess maybe those things are a little bit offside, I guess, maybe get to some people. I guess, you and nation are strange things. A lot of people don't want to think it's right. So I guess that's what you would do.
Did the New Orleans men impress you with their improvisation? Because they worked more as improvisational musicians, didn't they then?
Yeah, they did. I'm going to tell people. When did you write Stockyard? While you were at the theater?

Yeah. And you'd work it out as a xylophone solo to start with? Yeah. Oh yeah. Yeah. I'd make up the, that's where I write a lot of numbers for the, the washboard band. I'd, uh, a lot of them on xylophone, yeah. Yeah. Yeah. I'd make up the, that's where I write a lot of numbers for the, the washboard band. I'd, uh, a lot of them on xylophone, yeah.

Yeah. I'd start with xylophone. Was Freddie working with you at the theater? No. I, uh, cutting Freddie about, uh, we, uh, dear And so I came along with him and so I used to drink with him and so Freddie would always say, I'm going to make a record with you. And I told him about this number I had. And so he asked. He said, well the first chance I get is we'll make that number. And I think that I got the date to Inc. Williams. I told Freddie about it and Freddie got the band together. And we rehearsed it up and through. I don't recall why we made it but we rehearsed, I remember rehearsing at Freddie's hand. I remember Vincent was in there. Vincent was from there and play with the band. And Camel on piano. And I can't tell. I think the Dodds brothers are playing
there. I'm not sure. And Jackson, Benjo, Charlie Jackson. Because he does the Salty Dog on
there. Oh yeah. I don't know whether, I couldn't say Jackson with Freddie. Freddie was from there. Jackson didn't even need music.
There was a story about Freddie not wanting to record. Was that true? Because people would
copy his style? Oh, that could have been true. But he didn't, he wasn't so particular about recording. Well he liked me very much and so it was easy for me to get into recording.

He recorded with Doc Cook too on his Marlick band. But he didn't do a lot of recording. You told me he did record with some of your small groups all the time. Yeah, small groups. You told him on that pile. Yeah.

Freddie could take just a little mediocre group and take that trumpet away where he could improvise and he could do things. I think that Louie was more of a stylist but he could do things. Freddie was. He seemed to have more tricks in store. More improvising. And more improvising.
Freddie was. How did they compare in that day? Did people think of Louie as being better? Or

Kepard as being better? Freddie was the favorite. And for Louie establishing. So Louie started, I think the first tune to make Louie was West End. And from then on, Louie came into his own and he started recording. But prior to this, Freddie Kepler had Chicago. And then Joe Sutler.
Joe Sutler you think could match pretty close to Kepler? Yeah, pretty close. And then Louie, Louie stepped up where we're both up. Yeah. He was recording. Strange that Sutler never got

properly recorded. No, he never did do very much. His work of the Edgar was on the ground. Yeah, the way they did with Kepard, the way they spotted him, was supposed to be a hokum man in those days, you call him. Outside man, hokum. He was ready to play with those hot dancers. He played down. And for the punch, then he called Freddie. He said Freddie would get up and take his jelly band. And he played over the band. And the band just went along and called him and some sort of a riff. And Boston they called it. But Freddie would just be outside man for the punch. And he'd take it on out. And he'd take it on out. And he'd go on out. Jimmy Wicks was a baby.
How did Oliver compare with?
Well, Freddie. Well, I think Freddie had more stuff than Joe.

But Joe was most of us more of a style. And Louis still is a blue chord man. And he was a blues artist chord. And a hot chord man. But Freddie was great on breaks. He was great on... I had some kind of a new sort of... He could blue also and some of the other things he could do. Now, another thing Freddie kept with you. I don't know whether it's on the record or not. They sent for Tim Brown. Sent for the farm at the... Oh... Coconut Grove in New York. Had a big band. And the rich, the millionaires came to his coconut grove. He was the biggest one of the spots of New York. And so, Tim Brown had heard of this Freddie Kaepern. And so, he went down to play this season. And he just was a rave there in the play. He was like New York. He was going back to Scaldrack in the first season.
Swetman told me that Freddie played with him for a while at a beach ballroom. And about 1919. Do you think that might have been the same time? Same period?
Yeah, that was... 1919 was there after the war. Yeah. About the same time.
So, maybe Swetman got him from...
From... Brown. Yeah. He had a... kind of a season with Tim Brown. Big Brown.
Well, did liquor finally get the... Oh...

Now, Freddie Kaepern when he was with Charlie Cook now. Every night he's a quart of whiskey. That's started out with. That's why I was the same thing. I played with Bradshaw there. At the Regal Theater. And he drank whiskey with a pitcher for us. Pitcher, whiskey. Drinking glass for us. Both of them have a tremendous man in there. And whiskey got both of them.
How could Keppert play a show if he couldn't read?
Well, Keppert could read. He could.
Well, you could teach it to him off the xylophone or he could read. Yeah.
Just played with him.
Did you hear him with the original Creole, the Bill Johnson's band? And they're on the stage?
No, I'm not gonna say... They played the first time I heard that. I never... That was... They had a fella... Entertainer. Who was his band. I'm quite sure. H.M. Prince.
I think was the fella. Yeah.

It was his band. And he did a song and dance or something. And this band backed him up. And I know they came... know they were since then they came into St. York. I was waiting to the Brook of Washington. And we could hear the Creole there in downtown. I don't think I did how to hear them. I don't think I did. But I think I heard them in a different, some other place.
Was that their tour about 1915 or 16? Yeah.
That was, you see, I was first at St. Louis was 13. 14. This was around 14. Oh, come on. Creole band.
Everybody knew that they had something there, huh? Oh, yeah. In downtown DeHern.
Oh, yeah.
Maybe Vinson was in that band. This band? No, that was the Creole band that you're talking about. Because he and Kepard knew each other well. They worked together. Yeah.
And Bill Johnson was in.
Yeah, Bill Johnson was kind of random. There was men here in the group. Yeah. All the theory, I think.
Yeah. There was a bandit player, I think, since then. Here, Omar. He had a little here, Little Mitch. There was men driving.

A band that, uh, Jolly got together for a tour. And, uh, it had been a band that belonged to a man by the name of Eldin or Eldridge or something like that. Do you remember anything about such a band? It would be in the, maybe in the late 20s. No, 26, 22. What's going on?
I know him in the handy, if I was to have a band together.
Isn't that long? A couple of weeks?
No, no. Only a few days, didn't sell out.
Yeah. Who was in that handy, uh, John Lowe band? Any idea? I don't know.
I really don't know. You said I made the first record with him, Joe Rule. I don't remember the last record with him.
You made the first record with Joe Rule. Yeah, I made the first record. Who else was in that bandit?
Oh, I can't remember. It was just a record date.
He talked about it, yeah.
He's gonna sit as one of the men.
Do you remember any, uh, New Orleans men around Chicago in 1990s? I don't know where Swetman came from, but he wasn't New Orleans. I don't think so.
I tell you, in 99, I didn't know, I was wearing short pants. Yeah. Wearing short pants. I didn't know much about anything. I was going to go to theaters.
Oh, I wondered if you had, uh, uh, there's a theory that a jelly roll might have been in town early, and that, uh, maybe Bechet was here as early as that, but I doubt it.

I don't think he was here that early. I don't, I, I, I, one time I knew General Roll real well. He used to tell me a lot about himself. I don't think he came up then. He came up, he came up in kind of between times. He didn't come up with the real New Orleans fellows. I think he came in between times. He was always, he was always a loner, you know?
First, yeah, first time we'd hear about him was at a place called the Richelieu. Club Richelieu.
Club Richelieu.

And it was called Pompeian, I think. Yeah, I know about that phrase. But that was, uh, that could have been on a second trip up, because, uh, that was, uh, maybe after the war. It was, uh, 1982 or something like that.

Well, I first heard of General Roll, through his number, the General Roll Blues. I think he must have written that General Roll Blues. Well, I think he had written that by 16, I believe, in 1960. It seemed like I played it, my first job, job, and I left Hampton, was in the Palastino, north of Virginia. I played trumpet. It looked like we played General Roll Blues. And was it written by that time, General Roll? Or was it?
I don't think it was published, that early. Yeah.
He was in Memphis, La Croix, in Chicago. I was 16, I mean. It seemed like I played General Roll Blues about, long about that time. But I'm not kidding.
In Memphis.

Yeah, and he had General Roll Blues. Yeah, I'm not sure. Uh-huh. Yeah, I'm not sure. That's why he came to Hampton to get it, uh, see what he could do with it. So he came to Chicago and rostered it to me.

If I didn't play in 16, I certainly played in 17, because 17 does, yeah, I joined the Oakland Ugly Show, and I know we played it in 17, but it looks like I played in 16. But I know we played in 17. I know well. Quite a hit then, wasn't it? Quite a number.
Nice, nice, nice, nice, nice, nice, nice, nice.
Now that was just an instrumental, it wasn't, no words. I never heard any words.
Oh, a jelly roll. Instrumental.
Yeah. Because later on, maybe somebody did put a word, but I don't remember.
Jelly himself didn't put any words.
No, no he didn't. It was a nice number. Then of course, that number, I used to get that number mixed up with the old Junkman Blues. Lucky Roberts wrote that.
Oh yeah. That,

that, Well, the first number I played on the trumpet when I left Hampton Institute. I knew I was getting lost in the second. I lived with the – what was those boys' names in Norfolk? Shad – there were some brothers that had a band. Shack? Not Collins. I was in California? No, no, in Norfolk, Virginia. That was Shack, that was Garfield Cotter, the Cotter boys. They were quite the good in Virginia, in Norfolk. And Garfield came from New York, you must have known Garfield, because he played with his club club. Garfield Cotter, he was the big fiddle. They were quite a musical family. They played around Norfolk.
How did they spell them?

Cotter, C-R-T-E-R, Cotter. His name was Garfield, one of the names Shack, one of the names Shag. So that's a musical family. You know, Norfolk, in the beginning, used to be quite a little town. We called it Little New York. I mean, people danced there, there was dance bands, had the old booths there, the booths there, go up to Chesapeake, I guess, on picnics. Norfolk was a Little New Orleans or a Little New York.
That's where Jenkins' home was too, wasn't it, in Norfolk?
Which Jenkins?
The Arpen home that so many musicians had.
Oh, maybe it was.
Maybe it was. I guess they were exposed to all this music. And that's how they happened to make it such an important part of the orphan training.
Maybe so. I will say that Norfolk was quite a musical town. Norfolk and Newport News. You don't hear much about those town, but they were ranked up.
They had a lot of summer excursions and such.

Oh, yes, they had plenty of it. So there was a lot of calls. And then there was Buckrow Beach and Bayshore Beach. They were kind of mostly went to Bayshore. Later on, they began to go to Buckrow Beach. It was quite a beach. Buckrow? Buckrow Beach. And you know, down in Virginia, they call it the Peninsula. There was a whole lot of water. And a whole lot of activity around there. A whole lot of activity. A whole lot. Then you get on the boat and go right up, overnight boat to Baltimore, right up to Chesapeake. And move back and forth. A lot of traffic right on the water. And then in the summertime, concerts.
How long did you play there?

Not very long. Not very long. I'll tell you why. Because I finished Hampton in May of 16. Well, I went right to Norfolk and played in the Paris theater. And it wasn't very long before I got a letter from Hampton, offered me two school jobs. One in Topeka to teach school bands. That's really what I wanted to do. And one in Florida. So I selected one in Florida.
This was before the Florida job? Before.

Before. I went there and taught the school bands. That's what I wanted to do. And I suppose if I hadn't gotten in the Army, I probably would have made my home in Florida because there was one of the trustees, Mr. Balsall, Cullicolor, that owned a lot of property. I made one of them. Owned a couple of orange groves. And he said, Mr. Balsall, I made one of them myself, my honor. Land was very cheap. Land was very cheap. And he said, next year, you'll get yourself a part of land. I showed you how to go on. He had a couple of orange groves. But the next year, I was in the man's army. And I never went back to Florida. But I liked that. I liked that.
I liked that.

segments.title: Fragment about a young woman performer
segments.summary: The recording opens mid-conversation with brief remarks about a young woman, her parents and who worked for her.

segments.title: Noone at the Rumbogie while Brown was in New York
segments.summary: The interviewer asks whether Brown was around when Jimmie Noone broadcast from the Rumbogie; Brown was in New York then, in the late 1930s.

segments.title: Noone's band at the Savoy in New York and the imposed players
segments.summary: Brown explains how New York bookers added local players to Noone's small band at the Savoy, including Big Green, which hurt his soft small-band style; the interviewer asks who else was in it.

segments.title: Noone's arrival from New Orleans and his low register
segments.summary: Brown describes Noone as a top low-register clarinettist with fine technique who was choosy about the bands he joined.

segments.title: Chicago clarinettists: Simeon, Nichols, Bonnie and Johnny Dodds
segments.summary: Brown names Simeon, Nichols and Bonnie, and Johnny Dodds as clarinettists he admired, noting Bonnie as an early tenor saxophonist.

segments.title: Coleman Hawkins arriving in Chicago and as a creator
segments.summary: Brown recalls Hawkins coming to Chicago, possibly earlier with Mamie Smith, and calls him the number one saxophonist and a creator like Louis and Duke.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet and the soprano saxophone, tuning and tone
segments.summary: They discuss Bechet's clarinet and soprano playing, his trip with Will Marion Cook, Brown's dislike of his soprano tone and intonation, and why audiences like slightly off-pitch sounds.

segments.title: Writing Stockyard Strut and the Keppard record date
segments.summary: Jasper Taylor tells how he wrote Stockyard Strut on xylophone, got Freddie Keppard to record it for Ink Williams, and who rehearsed in the band.

segments.title: Keppard compared with Louis Armstrong and Joe Oliver
segments.summary: Taylor says Keppard improvised more and was Chicago's favourite before Louis rose, and compares his breaks and style with Oliver's.

segments.title: Keppard at the Coconut Grove with Tim Brown
segments.summary: Taylor describes Keppard's season with Tim Brown's big band at the Coconut Grove in New York, dated about 1919.

segments.title: Keppard's drinking and whether he could read music
segments.summary: Taylor says whiskey ruined Keppard and Bradshaw, and that Keppard could read music or learned by ear.

segments.title: Hearing the Original Creole Band and Bill Johnson
segments.summary: Taylor recalls first hearing the Creole band about 1914 on its tour, backing an entertainer, with Bill Johnson and Keppard.

segments.title: A touring band for Handy and Taylor's first record with Joe Rule
segments.summary: The interviewer asks about a short-lived touring band and its members; Taylor cannot remember them, only that he made the first record.

segments.title: New Orleans musicians in early Chicago and Jelly Roll Morton's arrival
segments.summary: Brown was a child around 1900; he recalls Jelly Roll as a loner who came up between waves of New Orleans players, and the Club Richelieu is mentioned.

segments.title: Playing Jelly Roll Blues and Junkman Blues in 1916-17
segments.summary: Brown and Taylor recall playing Jelly Roll Blues around 1916-17, when Brown left Hampton, whether it was published, and mix it up with Lucky Roberts's Junkman Blues.

segments.title: Norfolk's musical families, beaches and excursions
segments.summary: Brown describes the Cotter brothers' band and Norfolk as a musical town, with its beaches, excursion boats and Jenkins's orphanage.

segments.title: Leaving Hampton and teaching school bands in Florida
segments.summary: After finishing Hampton in May 1916 Brown played in Norfolk, then took a Florida job teaching school bands until the Army intervened.
